title: Air India To Induct Over 100 New Jets in 2027 and 2028
excerpt: CEO Campbell Wilson confirmed the fleet expansion at an employee townhall, as the Tata-owned carrier pushes ahead with its $400 million retrofit programme despite geopolitical headwinds.
body:
• Air India Group plans to add more than 100 new aircraft across Air India and Air India Express in 2027 and 2028.
  • The airline's $400 million widebody retrofit programme is underway, with 16 Boeing 787-8 aircraft scheduled for refurbishment in 2027.
  • Pakistani airspace closure has added up to three hours on key Europe and North America routes, increasing operational costs.
  • Widebody technical dispatch reliability has reached 97.4 per cent, and the carrier has added new Maharaja Club lounges, Wi-Fi, and upgraded cabins.

Air India Group will induct more than 100 new aircraft in 2027 and 2028, CEO Campbell Wilson told employees at a company townhall on August 14. The expansion covers both Air India and its low-cost arm Air India Express, as the Tata Group-owned carrier accelerates a fleet transformation that ranks among the largest in commercial aviation history.

Fleet Transformation in Motion

The numbers behind the overhaul are staggering. Air India placed orders for 470 aircraft with Airbus and Boeing in 2023, a deal worth roughly $70 billion. In December 2024, it followed up with a firm order for 100 more Airbus jets — 90 narrowbody A320-family aircraft and 10 widebody A350s — bringing the total order book to 570 planes.

Wilson said the airline continues to advance its fleet transformation despite a challenging operating environment. Three new Boeing 787-9 aircraft have already joined the fleet in 2026, and two Airbus A350-1000 widebodies are expected before year-end.

The Retrofit Programme

Alongside new deliveries, a $400 million legacy fleet retrofit programme is reshaping what passengers experience onboard. The narrowbody retrofit is complete. On the widebody side, three refurbished Boeing 787-8 aircraft have entered service this year, with four more expected before December. An additional 16 Boeing 787-8s are scheduled for retrofit in 2027, which would bring the 787-8 fleet refurbishment close to completion by year-end.

"With India's passenger growth outpacing the rest of the world, its significantly improving infrastructure and an aspirational young population increasingly going global, we see a clear case for Air India to expand its future fleet."

— Natarajan Chandrasekaran, Chairman, Tata Sons and Air India

Customer response to the upgraded fleet has been positive. Investments in new cabins, food and beverage offerings, Maharaja Club lounges, a refreshed loyalty programme, inflight entertainment, and onboard Wi-Fi have contributed to improved sentiment. Widebody technical dispatch reliability has climbed to 97.4 per cent.

Operating Through Turbulence

The expansion comes against a backdrop of industry-wide headwinds. Over the past six months, airlines globally have contended with higher jet fuel prices, geopolitical tensions, airspace disruptions, and currency depreciation. For Indian carriers, the closure of Pakistani airspace has added up to three hours on several key routes to Europe and North America, while disruptions from the Iran conflict have compounded operational complexity and fuel costs.

Wilson noted that softer demand on the India-US corridor has added to the pressure. But the airline has used temporary network curtailments from airspace restrictions to accelerate engineering work — advancing three major widebody maintenance checks, adding six rejuvenation lines, and introducing an additional Boeing production line for faster retrofit execution.

What This Means for Diaspora Travellers

For the millions of Indian Americans, British Indians, and Canadian Indians who fly between their adopted homes and India each year, Air India's expansion carries direct implications. More aircraft means more frequencies on high-demand corridors like New York–Delhi, San Francisco–Bangalore, and London–Mumbai. Upgraded cabins and modern widebodies replace the aging fleet that had long been a source of passenger frustration.

The airline also announced that annual salary increments for all employees, including ground staff and cabin crew, will take effect from October 1, 2026. The increment cycle had been deferred earlier this year due to the impact of the Middle East crisis. Revised pilot remuneration will also come into effect on the same date.

Air India's trajectory marks a sharp reversal from the debt-laden carrier that Tata Group acquired in January 2022. With 570 aircraft on order and a retrofit programme that is visibly changing the onboard product, the airline is betting that scale, modern equipment, and improved service can win back travellers who had written it off.
